name: Bilal Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior designer at Signal & Co, a small agency of nine that makes online ads and landing pages for shops that sell online: trainers, candles, protein powder. My day is building ad variations and page layouts, and testing which ones get more clicks. I use AI every day, for image drafts, for copy ideas, for resizing. Lena, the creative director, says I'm quick but I don't always know when something's good enough to send.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the numbers. You change a button colour and see sales go up by two percent the next morning, it's addictive. What wears me out is that ad work is a treadmill, fifty versions a week and nobody remembers any of them. On the side I sell design templates online, which makes about three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was overcooked, but the tools are still handy. I'd post a short video about which ones I'd keep paying for. At work I'd say let's use what works and stop chasing every new thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me fine. I'm already quicker than most juniors because of the tools. If the AI tools stall, my edge stays, and I get time to learn judgement from my creative director.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Signal & Co and keep the template shop ticking over. I'd put another chunk into my shares account, maybe two thousand. I'd ask Lena to let me sit in on client strategy calls so I learn what good looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything else on your mind in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sara, my girlfriend, wants us to buy somewhere in a year or two. She's a physiotherapist, so her job's steady. With my savings, about nine months' worth, and the shares, we're in decent shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the template shop survive a plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, it's small and steady. People still want a nice ready-made menu or invitation. I'd keep adding a few templates a month.

steps.text: Put another two thousand into his shares account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but in a friendly way. At work I'd offer to show people how I use the tools. Online I'd post how-tos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of juniors go, and I'd be one of the few kept, because I'm the one who makes the tools work. But I'm not stupid, Lena could also just use them herself. I'd be safe-ish for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate as much of the ad variation work as I can and pitch it to Lena as a service we sell. I'd grow the template shop, maybe to a thousand a month, using AI to make more templates. And I'd invest a bit more in shares of the AI companies, since that's where the money goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'm fine, but I can see friends getting squeezed. And I know safe-ish isn't safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if people lose jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, no one. It's how businesses work, if something's cheaper, they use it. Maybe the government should help people retrain, but I wouldn't blame the companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a junior who's struggling with the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to spend one evening a week just playing with the tools, no pressure. I'd show them my setup. Most of the AI tools aren't hard, people are just scared of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and we need sensible rules, quickly. At work I'd say we should change what we sell, before clients figure out they don't need us. Online I'd share what's working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the agency doesn't survive by 2028 in its current form. Clients would just ask the AI for their ads. My template shop dies too, because anyone can make a template in seconds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell most of my shares in the first months and keep the cash. I'd look for a role on the business side, like helping shops run their online stores, while there's still a human role. And in the three years before robots, I'd look at something physical, maybe product photography studios or packing for e-commerce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's my job and my side income at once. But Sara's work is hands-on and people-facing, and we've got savings, so we'd be okay for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap before robots mean for Sara and you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my girlfriend's physio work is safe until 2031 at least, because people want a human hand on their back. My work is all screen, so I'm hit in 2028. She'd carry us for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about Sara carrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weird. I've always been the one with the side hustle and the shares. But we'd be fine. I'd make myself useful at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance to get ahead of it. I'd post about how to build a business on top of AI. At work I'd say let's pivot now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to make good money first. I'd ride the tools for three or four years, then move before 2031. The design job still goes, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Lena to start an AI ad service, with me running it. I'd save hard, maybe a third of my pay. By 2029 I'd look at starting a small e-commerce shop myself, selling physical things, because selling stuff lasts longer than designing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too. It's a race and I like races.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after robots arrive, around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope my shop's running by then, mostly automated. If the robots do the packing, fine, I own the robots. That's the idea, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't owning a shop also risky when AI does everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. Big companies could crush me. But owning something beats being a junior designer in a world with no junior designers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. I'd post about long-term plans and investing. At work I'd say let's build something that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well. Ten years of being good with the tools is ten years of extra money. By 2036 I'd be 37, with savings, a shop, and Sara's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Signal & Co for three or four years, pushing the AI work. I'd keep investing every month and grow the template shop until it stops working. Then I'd start my own online business. We'd buy the flat in the first two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's coming, but I'd feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you nervous in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my shares crashed. Or if Sara's clinic got bought out. Otherwise, I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger designers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger designers not to fall in love with the job title. A job title is just a label. Learn to sell things, and learn the tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my job and my side income go at the same time. What would help is cheap loans for people starting small businesses, and clear rules so big platforms don't crush them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the fun. I actually enjoy this. I'd be scared and having fun at the same time, and I think lots of people my age are like that.

headlineQuote: I'd be scared and having fun at the same time, and I think lots of people my age are like that.
portrait: Bilal is a **junior ad designer** at a nine-person agency for online shops.
He uses **AI daily** and runs a small **template shop** on the side.
He's pragmatic, blames **no one**, and prefers owning to working for others.
His partner's **physio job** steadies the household in the fast scenarios.
He swings from **calm** to anxious and back to **uneasy** with time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job and side income vanish together.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small business starters and rules stopping **platforms** crushing them.
